name: 1994 January Anik E2 Failure

phenomena.details: Geomagnetic activity was only modest (Dst ~ −40 nT, WDC Kyoto). The event was a coronal-hole high-speed solar-wind stream that drove a sustained enhancement of relativistic (>2 MeV) electrons in the outer radiation belt.

impacts.description: Telesat Canada's Anik E1 and E2 communications satellites suffered momentum-wheel control failures from electrostatic discharge caused by deep dielectric charging in the enhanced relativistic-electron environment. Anik E1 (which failed first) was recovered within hours; Anik E2 lost attitude control and was out of service for about six months before engineers restored it with a ground-commanded backup control scheme. A textbook 'killer electron' satellite-failure case, alongside Telstar 401 (1997).
Loss of Anik E2 disrupted Canadian broadcast, telephone, and data services for an extended period; backup capacity had to be arranged across multiple satellites.

papers.title: The Anik satellite failures of 1994 January: What happened and why
papers.keyFinding: Attributed the Anik E1 and E2 failures to electrostatic discharge caused by deep dielectric charging from sustained elevated relativistic electron fluxes in the outer radiation belt.

papers.title: Anik-E1 and E2 satellite failures of January 1994 revisited
papers.authors: Lam, H.-L., Boteler, D. H., et al.
papers.keyFinding: Re-examined the 1994 Anik failures, reinforcing the coronal-hole high-speed-stream and relativistic-electron deep-dielectric-charging origin, with only modest geomagnetic (Dst) activity at the time.

summary: In January 1994 a coronal-hole high-speed stream drove sustained relativistic-electron flux that, through deep dielectric charging, knocked out attitude control on Telesat Canada's Anik E1 and E2 – despite only modest geomagnetic activity (Dst ~ −40 nT) – a textbook demonstration that satellite-damaging conditions do not require an intense ring-current storm.
description: In mid-to-late January 1994, during the descending phase of Solar Cycle 22, a long-lived coronal hole drove persistent high-speed solar-wind streams. Large-amplitude Pc5 ULF waves accelerated outer-belt electrons, producing roughly ten days of very high relativistic (>2 MeV) electron flux. Geomagnetic activity itself was only modest – WDC Kyoto Dst reached about −40 nT. On January 20, 1994 this electron environment caused deep dielectric (internal) charging and electrostatic discharge in Telesat Canada's Anik E1 and E2 geostationary satellites: Anik E1 lost momentum-wheel control but was recovered within hours, while Anik E2 was disabled for about six months before engineers restored it with a ground-based attitude-control workaround that required re-pointing roughly 100,000 receiving dishes. The same interval also disrupted the Intelsat-K satellite. The Anik failures are a landmark 'killer electron' case study, showing that deep dielectric charging from sustained relativistic-electron flux – not a deep Dst storm – can be the dominant satellite hazard.
